beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Surya, and this video is about one line of code that decided who was a teacher, and why the way it decided was wrong.

show.event: title snaps in, signal rule above, mono subtitle READING AN LTI ROLE

beats.narration_text: When Canvas launches our tool, the signed token carries a roles claim. It is a list, and the entries are not words. They are identifiers, written as full URNs. Our job is to turn that list into one decision: is this person a student, or do they run the course.

show.event: a full-width role URN, then a downward arrow to a signal decision block

beats.narration_text: The quick way to do that is to ask whether the text contains the word Instructor. It is one line, it reads naturally, and it passes every test you would think to write.

show.event: the one-line check in a bordered box, caption beneath

beats.narration_text: The problem is what else contains that word. A role identifier ending in PseudoInstructor contains it. So does one that is simply named badly. The check is not asking what the role is. It is asking whether those ten letters appear anywhere at all, and that is a different question.

show.event: three strings stacked, the matching substring picked out in signal

beats.narration_text: The meaning of a role URN is not spread through the string. It sits in the last segment, after the final slash or hash. Everything before it is namespace. So the right question is not does this contain Instructor. It is does the final segment equal one of the identifiers we accept.

show.event: one long URN with the namespace dimmed and the final segment boxed in signal

beats.narration_text: So we split on the separator, take the final segment, lowercase it, and look it up in a set of the identifiers we actually recognise. Instructor, Teaching Assistant, Content Developer, Administrator. Anything not in that set is a student. It fails closed, which is the direction you want a mistake to fall.

show.event: a vertical pipeline of four stages, then a filled signal terminal row

beats.narration_text: And then the escalation strings become test cases. Those three go in as inputs that must come back as student, so the next person who finds the one-line version attractive has to make them pass first.

show.event: three test inputs with their expected results

beats.narration_text: One line became four, and the four say what they mean. Substring matching is not a cheap version of an allow list. It is a different check that happens to agree with it most of the time.

show.event: two contrasting full-width rows, then the title restated
